entries.topic: Brent crude spot price
entries.finding: Brent crude rose to USD 83.55/bbl on 07-Aug-2026, +1.29% on the day, +7.09% on the month and +25.47% year-on-year. Price action in early August was dominated by Iran-Oman negotiations over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
entries.source_name: Trading Economics — Brent Crude Oil
entries.consequence: Anchors the crude input to the UAE monthly retail fuel price formula and therefore the revenue-per-litre driver. Sets the base of the 2026-2030 price path.

entries.topic: WTI crude spot price
entries.finding: WTI rose to USD 78.18/bbl on 07-Aug-2026 (+1.15% d/d). 52-week range: intraday low USD 54.97 on 17-Dec-2025 to intraday high USD 119.47 on 09-Mar-2026 — an exceptionally wide band reflecting the 2026 Iran conflict.
entries.source_name: Forbes Advisor — Crude Oil Price Today (via search); Trading Economics
entries.consequence: Cross-check on the crude benchmark; the WTI-Brent spread inverted for the first time since 2009 in April 2026, a signal of Middle East supply disruption rather than US-centric dynamics.

entries.topic: 2026 YTD crude oil price path — the Strait of Hormuz shock
entries.finding: Brent opened 2026 near USD 63 and rose to ~USD 70.69 by end-January. February ranged USD 63-72. In March the 2026 Iran war erupted: WTI gained 35% in one week (largest weekly gain since the contract began in 1983) and Brent climbed 28% to USD 92.69, breaching USD 100 and approaching USD 120 as Iran threatened Strait of Hormuz shipping. Prices peaked near USD 126 in April, then fell 13-16% on a ceasefire announcement; April range USD 83-111. May-June oscillated USD 84-114; by late June Brent fell below USD 70 as tankers resumed Hormuz transits. Renewed tension pushed Brent back above USD 100 on 23-Jul-2026. By early August prices stabilised at USD 82-83 on hopes of a full Hormuz reopening.
entries.source_name: Wikipedia — 2026-2028 world oil market chronology
entries.consequence: CRITICAL context. The 2026 crude path is not a normal cycle — it is a geopolitical shock centred on the Strait of Hormuz, through which the UAE's own exports transit. It drove UAE retail fuel prices up >60% since late February, which mechanically inflates ADNOC Distribution's revenue per litre and (via the ADNOC supply agreement) its inventory gains. Any forecast that extrapolates 2026 realised revenue or margin without decomposing this shock will be wrong. Also note: a Hormuz closure is a two-sided risk to a UAE downstream name — it lifts price but threatens physical supply.

entries.topic: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook — Brent forecast 2026-2027
entries.finding: July 2026 STEO: Brent averaged USD 85/bbl in June 2026 (down USD 22 from May and USD 32 from the April 2026 peak). Forecast Brent averages USD 74/bbl in 3Q26 and falls to USD 70/bbl in 4Q26 (USD 19/bbl lower than the June STEO). For 2027 Brent is forecast to average USD 65/bbl, USD 15/bbl lower than the June STEO. Earlier in the year (April 2026 STEO) EIA had raised its 2026 Brent projection to USD 96/bbl.
entries.source_name: US EIA July 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook (via Oil & Gas Journal and EIA pressroom)
entries.consequence: The official forecast is for a sharp mean-reversion in crude — Brent USD 70 by 4Q26 and USD 65 in 2027 versus USD 83.55 spot. If that path realises, UAE retail fuel prices fall materially from the August 2026 level, revenue per litre compresses, AND the ADNOC backstop mechanism (see CO-09) is triggered on retail inventory. This is a strong argument against extrapolating H1-2026 realised revenue. NOTE: the EIA PDF itself could not be parsed directly (binary); figures are taken from EIA-sourced secondary reporting and should be re-verified against the STEO tables before use as a build driver.

entries.topic: Global refined-product cracks / refining margins 2025-2026
entries.finding: Crack spreads hit record highs in 2026. The prompt NYMEX 3-2-1 crack spread reached a record USD 64.58/bbl on 08-Jul-2026 (Reuters data). European diesel refining margins reached a record above USD 60/bbl after Russia halted diesel exports amid a domestic fuel crisis worsened by Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries; European gasoline traded at a four-year-high premium over crude of USD 41/bbl. Earlier in the year the picture was softer: in early February 2026 Singapore 95 RON gasoline cracks fell USD 1.61/bbl w/w, Singapore ULSD cracks fell USD 0.71/bbl and jet/kero USD 1.09/bbl, with US and Asian margins dragged lower by softer gasoil/diesel values.
entries.source_name: Forbes — Refining Stocks Soar As Crack Spread Hits Record High In 2026; Kpler; IndexBox
entries.consequence: Record cracks are a refiner story, not directly a fuel-retailer story: ADNOC Distribution buys product from ADNOC under a supply agreement, so high cracks raise its input cost. However the UAE monthly pricing formula explicitly incorporates international refining margins, so record cracks flow into the retail price and hence into revenue per litre. Relevant to the price-side driver, and a caution against assuming retail price moves track crude alone.

entries.topic: Global EV penetration trajectory
entries.finding: IEA Global EV Outlook 2026 (published May 2026): global electric passenger car sales exceeded 20 million units in 2025, reaching 25% of all new car sales for the first time. IEA projects 23 million units in 2026, ~28% of total global car sales.
entries.unit: % of global new car sales (2026 forecast)
entries.source_name: IEA Global EV Outlook 2026
entries.consequence: The global terminal-value driver for fuel retail. Sets the outer bound on long-run fuel volume growth and is the primary justification for a conservative terminal growth rate and for weighting the non-fuel/convenience leg. NOTE: UAE penetration is materially different (see I-08) — do not apply the global number to the UAE fleet.

entries.topic: Non-fuel income share at global fuel-retail peers
entries.finding: Across the US convenience/fuel-retail industry, inside sales drive roughly 70-78% of gross profit despite being only ~22% of revenue. Industry revenue split: fuel ~USD 520bn (76% of revenue) at 2-4% gross margin; in-store merchandise ~USD 148bn (22%) at 32-38% gross margin; foodservice ~USD 12bn (2%) at 48-58% gross margin. Casey's General Stores reported an inside margin of 41.5% and a fuel margin of 38.7 US cents per gallon (ex credit-card fees) for fiscal 2025. At Couche-Tard, in-store merchandise and prepared food contribute a larger share of gross profit than fuel despite lower volumes; Q1 FY2026 merchandise and service gross profit was USD 1.7bn.
entries.unit: % of gross profit from non-fuel (70-78% at US peers)
entries.source_name: Raymond James Convenience Store Insight; Couche-Tard corporate releases; Casey's FY2025 SEC-filed release
entries.consequence: The structural benchmark against which ADNOC Distribution's non-fuel leg must be judged. ADNOC Distribution's non-fuel gross profit was USD 140m in H1-2026 versus H1 total EBITDA of USD 786m — far below the 70-78% peer benchmark, i.e. it remains a fuel-led business with a long non-fuel runway. This gap is the central growth-vs-terminal-value tension in the study and a candidate for the §1.7 crux.

entries.topic: US Federal Reserve policy rate — drives UAE rates via the AED/USD peg
entries.finding: The FOMC held the federal funds target range at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent (3.50%-3.75%) at its meeting concluded 29-Jul-2026. The vote was 9-3, with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissenting IN FAVOUR OF A QUARTER-POINT INCREASE. The Committee has held at every meeting in 2026 after three cuts in the final months of 2025. Effective rate ~3.63% as of June 2026.
entries.source_name: Federal Reserve Board — FOMC statement, 29 July 2026
entries.consequence: The AED is pegged to the USD, so the Fed sets the floor for UAE money-market rates and hence the CBUAE Base Rate (C-05) and ADNOC Distribution's floating-rate debt cost. Note the hawkish direction of travel: three dissents for a HIKE, and markets pricing a 25bp increase in September 2026 (see G-09). A rising-rate path is the opposite of what a standard EM cost-of-capital build would assume and must be priced explicitly in the WACC discussion.

entries.topic: US 10-year Treasury yield
entries.finding: The US 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.65% on 07-Aug-2026 and held around 4.68% on Friday 08-Aug-2026. Fed officials have increasingly signalled readiness to raise rates amid mounting inflationary pressure, with markets pricing a 25bp hike in September 2026.
entries.source_name: Trading Economics — US 10 Year Treasury Note Yield
entries.consequence: Because AED is pegged and UAE federal paper prices at a few basis points over comparable USTs (see C-06), the UST curve is the effective backbone of the AED risk-free rate. A UAE/Abu Dhabi 10Y USD point marked off today's UST 10Y at the Feb-2026 issue spread of +25bp implies ~4.90-4.93%.

entries.topic: UAE real GDP growth 2025 actual
entries.finding: IMF: UAE GDP projected to expand 4.8% in 2025, driven by non-hydrocarbon growth of 4.6% and a 5.3% rebound in hydrocarbon GDP. World Bank estimate: 5.6% in 2025, with non-oil growth 6.1% and oil sector 4.1%. CBUAE separately estimated 4.9% for 2025.
entries.source_name: IMF — 2025 Article IV Consultation, United Arab Emirates (Staff Report and press release)
entries.consequence: Macro backdrop for UAE fuel-volume growth. Note the spread across official sources (4.8% IMF vs 5.6% World Bank) — do not present a single point without naming the source.
entries.staleness: STALE (as_of 02-Oct-2025, >6 months old) — the IMF 2026 Article IV was not located; re-verify before use as a driver

entries.topic: UAE real GDP growth 2026-2027 forecast, non-oil specifically
entries.finding: IMF: 2026 growth projected to accelerate to 5.0%, driven by stronger hydrocarbon GDP (6.3%) with non-hydrocarbon GDP stable at 4.6%. CBUAE forecasts 5.6% for 2026 (an earlier CBUAE vintage said 5.3%). A 2027 official forecast could not be sourced.
entries.source_name: IMF 2025 Article IV; CBUAE Quarterly Economic Review
entries.consequence: Non-oil GDP growth of ~4.6% is the closest macro proxy for UAE fuel demand growth. It should be reconciled against the company's own realised UAE volume growth of +1.6% y/y in H1-2026 (CO-04) — volumes are growing far slower than non-oil GDP, which is the single most important sanity check on any volume driver. Do not set volume growth off GDP without that reconciliation.
entries.staleness: STALE (as_of 02-Oct-2025) — 2026-2027 forecasts predate the 2026 oil shock entirely and must be re-verified

entries.topic: UAE CPI inflation 2025 actual and 2026-2027 forecast
entries.finding: Inflation averaged 1.3% in 2025, with declines in transport costs and textile prices and favourable food prices. December 2025 CPI rose 2.04% y/y, up from 1.61% in November. CBUAE projects headline inflation of 1.8% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027.
entries.source_name: Central Bank of the UAE — Quarterly Economic Review, March 2026
entries.consequence: The domestic escalator for genuinely domestic cost lines (UAE wages, local services, station opex). Per the cost-stack escalation rule, this 1.8-2.0% domestic CPI must NOT be applied to product-cost or globally-traded input lines — those escalate on their own commodity path. Note the CBUAE 2026 forecast of 1.8% predates the >60% retail fuel price surge since late February 2026 and is very likely to be revised upward; transport is a CPI component.
entries.staleness: CURRENT (Mar-2026), but the forecast predates the 2026 fuel-price surge — flag as likely superseded

entries.topic: UAE population growth and vehicle parc / registrations
entries.finding: UAE vehicle registrations reached 4.56 million by June 2025, up from 4.17 million a year earlier — +9.35% y/y, equal to ~390,000 additional vehicles. New car registrations were ~157,000 units in H1-2025, +11% vs H1-2024. Dubai: RTA reports up to 3.5 million vehicles circulating during daytime hours, +10% in two years versus a global average of 2-4%; Dubai population grew by more than 208,000 residents over the year, and Q2-2025 registrations rose 2%. Structural shift: 15-17% of all new car registrations in H1-2025 were Chinese brands, and 67% of all EVs sold in the UAE were Chinese.
entries.source_name: Khaleej Times / The Filipino Times (citing UAE Ministry of Interior and Dubai RTA data); DubiCars UAE Automotive Industry Report
entries.consequence: The physical volume driver: vehicle parc growth of ~9% y/y sits far above the company's realised +1.6% H1-2026 fuel volume growth. That gap (parc +9%, volumes +1.6%) is a material tension — candidate explanations are fleet efficiency, EV substitution, market-share loss, or price elasticity following the >60% price rise. This should be resolved explicitly in the driver build, not averaged over. A parc-based volume driver alone would materially overstate volumes.
entries.staleness: STALE (as_of Jun-2025, 14 months old). No 2026 vehicle-parc update could be sourced — flag as a gap.

entries.topic: UAE Central Bank Base Rate
entries.finding: CBUAE has maintained the Base Rate applicable to the Overnight Deposit Facility (ODF) at 3.65%. The most recent confirmation of the hold was announced on 29-Jul-2026 (following the FOMC), with earlier holds through March, April and June 2026; the level dates from the decision announced 18-Mar-2026. The Base Rate is anchored to the US Fed's IORB and provides an effective floor for overnight money-market rates in the UAE. The rate on short-term liquidity borrowing from CBUAE remains 50bp above the Base Rate for all standing credit facilities.
entries.source_name: Central Bank of the UAE — 'CBUAE Maintains the Base Rate at 3.65%'
entries.consequence: The policy anchor for AED short rates and the floor for floating-rate bank debt pricing (EIBOR-linked term loans). Not itself the risk-free rate for a DCF — use the federal T-bond curve (C-06) for that — but it constrains the marginal cost of short-dated debt.

entries.topic: UAE federal AED Treasury Bond curve — THE RISK-FREE ANCHOR
entries.finding: July 2026 auction (results announced ~30-Jul-2026): the Ministry of Finance completed the July 2026 auctions of UAE dirham-denominated Treasury Islamic Sukuk and Treasury Bonds, issuing AED 1.1bn. Yields to maturity were 4.49% for the October 2027 T-Sukuk tranche and 4.48% for the January 2031 T-Bond tranche. These corresponded to spreads of 24bp and 4bp respectively above comparable US Treasuries at the time of issuance. Total bids AED 4.83bn, 4.4x oversubscribed.
entries.unit: % YTM, AED federal T-Bond maturing January 2031 (~4.5 year tenor)
entries.source_name: UAE Ministry of Finance / WAM (Emirates News Agency) — July 2026 Treasury Sukuk and Bonds auction results
entries.consequence: PRIMARY RISK-FREE ANCHOR for an AED-denominated DCF. This is a local-currency government yield from the sovereign's own curve, exactly as the WACC rule requires (rf from the LOCAL govt bond even for pegged currencies — never shortcut to USD). Under the v2 method, rf* = local govt-bond yield minus that sovereign's OWN adjusted default spread: 4.48% - 0.42% = 4.06% normalised rf at the ~4.5y point. Country risk then enters ONCE via the CRP inside the ERP. NOTE the tenor gap: the longest AED federal point available is Jan-2031 (~4.5y), NOT 10 years. The UAE has not issued a 10-year AED T-bond as of this sweep. A 10-year AED point must therefore be extrapolated (see C-08 for the USD 10Y evidence) and that extrapolation must be disclosed as a construction, not presented as an observed yield.

entries.topic: UAE federal AED T-Bond curve — prior auctions (path evidence)
entries.finding: May 2026 auction: AED 1.1bn issued, YTM 4.03% for the T-Bond tranche maturing September 2027 and 4.30% for the tranche maturing January 2031. An earlier vintage (undated in the source) recorded 3.73% for September 2027 and 3.85% for January 2031, and treasury sukuk YTMs of 3.53% for May 2030 and 3.779% for February 2033. March 2026 auction: AED 1.1bn issued (yields not disclosed in the sourced material).
entries.source_name: UAE Ministry of Finance — 'UAE Successfully Concludes May 2026 Treasury Bond Auction'
entries.consequence: Shows the AED curve rising through 2026 (Jan-2031 point: 3.85% in an earlier vintage, 4.30% in May-2026, 4.48% in Jul-2026). Confirms the July print is not an outlier and that the direction of travel is upward, consistent with the hawkish Fed. Reinforces that a stale rf from an older vintage would understate the discount rate by ~45bp.

entries.topic: Abu Dhabi sovereign USD bond — 10-year point
entries.finding: Abu Dhabi's February 2026 dual-tranche USD issuance raised USD 3bn. The 10-year tranche priced with a 4.25% coupon at a reoffer price of 99.814%, yield 4.73%, spread +25bp over US Treasuries (tightened from IPTs in the +55bp area). The 5-year tranche priced at a 3.75% coupon, 99.824% reoffer, +20bp over USTs. Combined orderbook peaked above USD 11bn, settling at USD 4.3bn for the short tenor and USD 5.6bn for the 10-year.
entries.unit: % yield at issue, Abu Dhabi 10-year USD sovereign, February 2026
entries.source_name: Zawya — 'Abu Dhabi raises $3bln as investor demand drives tight spreads on dual-tranche bond'; Abu Dhabi Department of Finance / Abu Dhabi Media Office
entries.consequence: The only observed 10-year sovereign point for the emirate in which ADNOC Distribution is domiciled. Because it is a February-2026 PRIMARY PRINT, not a live secondary yield, it is a stale level — but the SPREAD (+25bp over UST) is the durable, transferable quantity. Marked off today's UST 10Y of 4.68% (G-09), an Abu Dhabi 10Y USD point today is approximately 4.93%. Use the spread, not the February yield level. A live secondary quote could not be sourced and this is recorded as a gap.
entries.staleness: STALE as a yield level (Feb-2026, 6 months old). The +25bp spread is treated as current; re-mark against live UST.

entries.topic: UAE sovereign credit rating — Moody's
entries.finding: Moody's affirmed the United Arab Emirates at Aa2 with a stable outlook on 12-Jun-2026, citing robust public finances, high per-capita income and effective policymaking ('strong shock-absorption capacity').
entries.source_name: The National — 'UAE retains high Moody's ratings and stable outlook on strong shock-absorption'
entries.consequence: Aa2 is the rating that maps to the Damodaran default spread of 0.42% used to normalise rf and to derive the CRP (C-13). It confirms the Damodaran row's rating input is current as at the valuation date, even though the Damodaran file itself is a January-2026 vintage.

entries.topic: UAE sovereign credit rating — S&P
entries.finding: S&P Global Ratings affirmed the UAE sovereign rating at AA/A-1+ for both local and foreign currency, with a stable outlook, on 06-Mar-2026.
entries.source_name: Gulf News — 'UAE earns top sovereign ratings from global agencies'
entries.consequence: Cross-check on the sovereign quality input. S&P at AA is one notch above the Moody's Aa2 equivalent; the study uses the Moody's row for consistency with the Damodaran file, and should say so.

entries.topic: UAE sovereign credit rating — Fitch
entries.finding: Fitch affirmed the UAE at AA- with a stable outlook on 23-May-2026.
entries.source_name: Gulf News — 'UAE earns top sovereign ratings from global agencies'
entries.consequence: Cross-check. The three agencies span AA- to AA (Aa2 equivalent), i.e. the UAE sits solidly in the AA band with all three — supporting a low single-digit-bp country risk premium rather than an EM-style premium.

entries.topic: Damodaran country risk premium — UNITED ARAB EMIRATES row, from the ORIGINAL ctryprem.html
entries.finding: Read live from the original file at pages.stern.nyu.edu. The file header reads verbatim: 'Last updated: January 5, 2026'. UNITED ARAB EMIRATES row: Moody's rating Aa2; Adjusted Default Spread 0.42%; Country Risk Premium 0.64%; Equity Risk Premium 4.87%. The file carries a separate ABU DHABI row with IDENTICAL figures (Aa2 / 0.42% / CRP 0.64% / ERP 4.87%). Other UAE emirates in the same file: Ras Al Khaimah (Emirate of) A3, default spread 1.02%, CRP 1.55%, ERP 5.78%; Sharjah Ba1, default spread 2.13%, CRP 3.24%, ERP 7.47%. US equity risk premium in the same file: 4.46%; US default spread 0.23%; implied mature-market ERP = 4.46% - 0.23% = 4.23%.
entries.unit: % total equity risk premium for UAE / Abu Dhabi
entries.source_name: Aswath Damodaran (NYU Stern) — Country Default Spreads and Risk Premiums (ctryprem.html), ORIGINAL FILE
entries.consequence: THE cost-of-equity input. Ke = rf* + beta x ERP, with rf* = 4.48% - 0.42% = 4.06% (C-06) and ERP = 4.87%. Country risk enters ONCE, via the 0.64% CRP embedded inside the 4.87% ERP — using the raw 4.48% local yield PLUS the CRP-loaded ERP would double-count sovereign risk (the v1 bug). Critically, the ABU DHABI row is identical to the UAE row, so no emirate-level adjustment is warranted for an Abu Dhabi-domiciled issuer — but note that Sharjah (7.47%) and RAK (5.78%) are materially higher, so 'UAE' is not a single risk block. Per the CONSISTENCY rule, strip the same basis of default spread as the CRP added back (rating-based here), and publish both ERP bases.
entries.staleness: FLAGGED — the ORIGINAL file is a 05-Jan-2026 vintage, ~7 months old at the valuation date. See C-13 for the mid-year update discrepancy.

entries.topic: Damodaran July-2026 mid-year update — DISCREPANCY FLAG
entries.finding: A Damodaran 'Equity Risk Premiums, by country - July 2026 Update' exists, published 03-Jul-2026, covering 157 markets and using a mature-market ERP of 4.17%, a US ERP of 4.45% and an equity volatility multiplier of 1.5545. The update notes state that a lower mature-market premium combined with lower sovereign default spreads pulled equity risk premiums down across the board; the regional 'Middle East' weighted average is quoted at 6.37%. HOWEVER: the ORIGINAL ctryprem.html file at pages.stern.nyu.edu still reads 'Last updated: January 5, 2026' with US ERP 4.46%, i.e. the canonical HTML file has NOT been refreshed to the July vintage as at 09-Aug-2026. The UAE row from the July-2026 workbook could NOT be verified from the original file. One secondary source reported an 'Abu Dhabi (UAE)' row of default spread 0.49%, CRP 0.66%, ERP 4.99%, Aa2 — this figure is UNVERIFIED against the original file and CONTRADICTS the original file's 0.42% / 0.64% / 4.87%; it must NOT be used.
entries.source_name: Aswath Damodaran — 'Equity Risk Premiums, by country - July 2026 Update' (LinkedIn); third-party summary at elitecurrensea.com
entries.consequence: FLAG-BEFORE-ISSUE item. The protocol requires the UAE row from the ORIGINAL ctryprem.html, and that file is the January-2026 vintage. Two defensible responses: (a) use the original-file row (4.87% ERP) and disclose that it is the January-2026 vintage; or (b) source the July-2026 workbook (ctryprem.xlsx) directly and re-read the UAE row. Option (b) is preferable and should be attempted before the build; if it cannot be reached, use (a) and state the vintage. Do NOT use the unverified 4.99% secondary figure. The ERP delta between vintages (4.87% vs a possible ~4.78-4.99%) is small but non-trivial in a WACC — this is a candidate for a stated sensitivity rather than a silent choice.

entries.topic: UAE federal corporate tax — 9% regime
entries.finding: The UAE corporate tax rate is 9%, charged on taxable profits above AED 375,000 annually, under the federal corporate tax regime. Businesses extracting UAE natural resources (oil, gas, minerals) remain subject to existing EMIRATE-LEVEL taxation and are carved out of the federal corporate tax net entirely; ADNOC subsidiaries engaged in upstream extraction fall under emirate-level fiscal arrangements rather than the 9% federal rate.
entries.source_name: PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries — United Arab Emirates, Corporate taxes on corporate income; UAE Ministry of Finance
entries.consequence: Tax rate driver for the FCFF waterfall. The upstream-extraction carve-out does NOT cover ADNOC Distribution: it is a downstream retail and distribution business, not an extractor, so it sits inside the federal net. See C-15 and C-16 for the higher effective rate that actually applies.

entries.topic: UAE Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (DMTT) — 15%
entries.finding: The UAE introduced a 15% Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax effective for financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2025, under Cabinet Decision No. (142) of 2024, following the December 2024 Ministry of Finance announcement. It applies to multinational enterprise groups with consolidated global revenues of EUR 750 million or more in at least two of the past four financial years, aligning the UAE with the OECD Pillar Two Global Minimum Tax. It is a top-up mechanism guaranteeing in-scope groups pay an effective tax rate of at least 15% on their UAE profits.
entries.source_name: UAE Ministry of Finance — Top-up Tax; EY Global Tax Alert; PwC Middle East
entries.consequence: MATERIAL TAX DRIVER. ADNOC Group's consolidated global revenues are far above the EUR 750m threshold, and ADNOC Distribution alone reported ~AED 40.8bn TTM revenue, so the DMTT threshold is clearly met at group level. The forecast tax rate for ADNOC Distribution should therefore be built at 15%, NOT 9% — a 6-percentage-point difference that flows straight through the FCFF waterfall and is worth several percent of equity value. This is a strong candidate for the dual-framing treatment (9% federal headline vs 15% DMTT effective) rather than a single assumed rate. MUST be confirmed against the company's own tax note in the audited filings before the build is fixed — the sweep establishes the regime, the filing establishes the realised rate.

entries.topic: UAE retail fuel pricing mechanism — deregulation and the monthly committee
entries.finding: The UAE Ministry of Energy deregulated fuel prices with effect from 1 August 2015, adopting a pricing policy linked to global prices. A Fuel Price Committee reviews prices against average international levels each month before implementation. The committee is chaired by the Undersecretary of the Ministry of Energy and includes as members the Undersecretary of the Ministry of Finance, the CEO of ADNOC Distribution, and the CEO of ENOC. On the 28th of each month the committee announces prices for the following month, based on average global prices plus operating costs. The mechanism deliberately does not rely on a single global market, and is designed to 'facilitate distribution companies to make reasonable profits and to limit their losses while offering premium services'. Each month the committee evaluates prevailing global benchmark crude prices, international refining margins and domestic operating costs to determine the retail price for each grade.
entries.source_name: UAE Cabinet — 'Fuel Prices to be deregulated with effect from 1 August, 2015'; The Official Portal of the UAE Government — Deregulation of fuel prices
entries.consequence: THE central pricing driver and the reason this business is not a normal price-taking retailer. Three consequences for the build: (1) retail price is a REGULATED PASS-THROUGH of global prices plus operating costs, reset monthly — so revenue per litre is formulaic and forecastable from a crude/crack path, not a competitive outcome; (2) the ADNOC Distribution CEO sits ON the committee, which is a governance fact worth disclosing; (3) the formula's explicit inclusion of operating costs plus the ADNOC supply-agreement backstop (CO-09) means the unit margin is structurally protected, which is the core argument for a lower cost of equity than a commodity-exposed comparable would carry. The deregulation date is 2015 and the mechanism is unchanged — 'stale' is not the right frame for a standing regime, but re-verify no 2025-2026 amendment exists.
entries.staleness: Regime in force since 2015 and unchanged as at Aug-2026; the mechanism description is standing, not a volatile figure

entries.topic: UAE retail fuel prices — August 2026 (current levels)

entries.topic: UAE retail fuel price path — full monthly 2026 series
entries.finding: Monthly UAE retail prices, AED/litre (Super 98 / Special 95 / E-Plus 91 / Diesel): January 2.53 / 2.42 / 2.34 / 2.55; February 2.45 / 2.33 / 2.26 / 2.52; March 2.59 / 2.48 / 2.40 / 2.72; April 3.39 / 3.28 / 3.20 / 4.69; May 3.66 / 3.55 / 3.48 / 4.69; June 3.95 / 3.83 / 3.76 / 4.33; July 3.40 / 3.29 / 3.21 / 3.60; August 3.60 / 3.49 / 3.41 / 3.80. Four distinct phases: declines through February, a supply-driven spike peaking in June, a sharp July correction, and a partial August recovery. Special 95 rose from the February low of 2.33 to the June peak of 3.83, +64%. Retail prices surged over 60% from late February before the temporary July decline. Diesel spiked hardest, to 4.69 in April-May (+86% from February), consistent with the record global diesel cracks in G-05.
entries.source_name: OneClickDrive UAE Petrol Prices 2026 Tracker (monthly compilation of UAE Fuel Price Committee announcements)
entries.consequence: The single most important external series in the study. It explains ADNOC Distribution's H1-2026 revenue growth of +29% on volume growth of only +1.6% — the revenue increase is almost entirely PRICE, not volume, and price is a regulated pass-through the company does not control. Any forecast that carries the H1-2026 revenue run-rate forward implicitly assumes crude stays near USD 83+; the EIA path (G-04) says USD 70 by 4Q26 and USD 65 in 2027, which would push retail prices back toward the AED 2.50-2.90 region. This is the study's most consequential contested judgement and a strong candidate for the mandatory both-ways dual-framing treatment. SECONDARY SOURCE CAUTION: this is a compiled tracker, not the Ministry of Energy's own publication; individual months should be spot-checked against the monthly announcements before being fixed as build inputs. The April and May diesel figure of 4.69 in particular sits far above the petrol grades and warrants a direct check.

entries.topic: UAE fuel retail market structure and shares
entries.finding: ADNOC Distribution, ENOC and Emarat jointly controlled about 85% of UAE retail fuel volumes in 2025. ADNOC Distribution operated 977 stations by Q3-2025 and is the largest network, present across all seven emirates. ENOC (founded 1993) had grown to 198 stations in the UAE as of 2024, managing over 116 Dubai locations including the former EPPCO stations (EPPCO is an ENOC group brand, not an independent third competitor). Emarat (Emirates General Petroleum Corporation, established 1981) operates ~100 stations across Dubai and the Northern Emirates. TotalEnergies also competes in the UAE retail market.
entries.unit: % of UAE retail volumes held by top three (2025)
entries.source_name: Mordor Intelligence — United Arab Emirates Fuel Station Market; ENOC and Emarat corporate sites
entries.consequence: A concentrated, geographically segmented market: ADNOC Distribution historically dominant in Abu Dhabi, ENOC/EPPCO in Dubai, Emarat in the Northern Emirates. With prices set uniformly by the Fuel Price Committee, competition is on network density and non-fuel offer only. Supports a stable market-share assumption in the volume driver and a low competitive-erosion risk, but also caps organic UAE volume upside — which is exactly why the growth story has moved to Saudi, Egypt and now South Africa. NOTE: EPPCO should NOT be modelled as a fourth independent competitor.

entries.topic: Saudi Arabia fuel retail — licensing and consolidation regime
entries.finding: All activities relating to petroleum and petrochemical materials require prior licensing from the Saudi Ministry of Energy under the Petroleum and Petrochemical Materials Law, which replaced the previous Law of Trade in Petroleum Products. The regime is intended to ensure security and reliability of supply and has driven consolidation of a historically fragmented station market. Vision 2030 is central, aiming to diversify the energy sector, modernise fuel infrastructure and integrate alternative energy; the government is promoting modern stations with automated dispensing, IoT monitoring and integrated retail services. In June 2026 the Ministry announced winning bidders for eight LPG filling, storage and bulk distribution licences.
entries.source_name: Saudi Press Agency; Zawya — 'Saudi: Energy Ministry mandates licenses for all petroleum, petrochemical operations'
entries.consequence: The licensing-driven consolidation of Saudi fuel retail is the structural opportunity ADNOC Distribution's Saudi expansion is built on: thousands of sub-scale independent stations must either upgrade to standard or exit, creating a branded-operator land grab. Supports the credibility of the Saudi station-count ramp (I-04) but also means the growth is regulatory-window-dependent, not perpetual — relevant to how long above-trend Saudi growth should be carried in the forecast.

entries.topic: ADNOC Distribution Saudi Arabia entry, network and competitors

Listed Saudi competitors: Aldrees Petroleum and Transport Services (Tadawul 4200) and Saudi Automotive Services Company / SASCO (Tadawul 4050).

It should be modelled as its own driver leg (sites x throughput x dealer margin), NOT blended into UAE economics. NOTE THE TARGET-DATE CONTRADICTION: earlier reporting said 300 stations by 2026, the H1-2026 call says 300 by 2029. Use the company's own most recent statement (2029) and flag the discrepancy; confirm against the company's H1-2026 disclosure pack.

entries.topic: Egypt fuel retail — TotalEnergies Marketing Egypt JV and EGP exposure
entries.finding: ADNOC Distribution completed the acquisition of a 50% stake in TotalEnergies Marketing Egypt LLC from TotalEnergies Marketing Afrique SAS in February 2023 (announced July 2022) for approximately USD 186 million, entering the Egyptian market. The portfolio comprised 240 fuel retail stations, 100+ convenience stores, 250+ lube-changing stations and car washes, plus wholesale fuel, aviation fuel and lubricant blending operations. The deal was expected to uplift ADNOC Distribution EBITDA by c.+6% on a fully-consolidated basis from year 1. The company plans to add ~6 stations annually in Egypt and added 1 Egypt site in H1-2026; it opened its first flagship New Cairo station in 2025. Management stated in the H1-2026 call that Egypt performance has exceeded the investment case and that '85%-90% of the business is naturally protected against any EGP devaluation', with aviation and lubricants the primary profit drivers.

entries.consequence: Egypt is the study's main FX-risk leg, and management's claim that 85-90% is naturally hedged against EGP devaluation is a MATERIAL, TESTABLE assertion that must be verified against the segment disclosure rather than accepted — the natural hedge comes from USD-linked aviation and lubricant revenue. If true, Egypt requires no EGP depreciation haircut on most of its cash flow; if not, the leg needs an explicit EGP path. Given Egypt's inflation and currency history this is a candidate for an explicit both-ways sensitivity. Note the 50% stake: confirm from the filings whether Egypt is consolidated or equity-accounted before building the leg.

entries.topic: EV charging in the UAE — policy targets and adoption
entries.finding: The UAE National Electric Vehicles Policy, under the Net Zero 2050 strategy, targets 50% of vehicles on the road to be electric by 2050 and ~10% by 2030, with incentives (free registration and parking, reduced fees) and fast-charging expansion; it also targets a 20% reduction in transport-sector energy consumption and a centralised national charging database, plus a government fleet of 42,000 EVs by 2030 and 30% of government procurement electric or hybrid by 2030. EV+PHEV share of new UAE car sales was ~13% in 2023 (up from ~3% in 2022), with adoption projected to grow 20-30% annually through 2030. 67% of all EVs sold in the UAE in H1-2025 were Chinese brands.
entries.unit: % of vehicles on the road targeted electric by 2030 (UAE policy)
entries.source_name: The Official Platform of the UAE Government — National Electric Vehicles Policy
entries.consequence: The terminal-value driver for the UAE fuel leg. The critical distinction for a 5-year horizon is STOCK versus FLOW: even at 13%+ of new SALES, the target is only ~10% of the vehicle PARC electric by 2030, and fuel volumes track the parc, not the sales mix. Over the study's 5-year explicit forecast the EV drag on UAE fuel volumes is therefore modest — low single-digit percent cumulatively — and the real EV exposure sits in the terminal value and in the offsetting charging-point build (the company guides 50-60 new EV charging points in 2026 and 10-15x more fast/super-fast points by 2028 vs a 2023 base). Model EV as a parc-share drag on volume, never as a new-sales-share drag. GAP: a 2025 or 2026 UAE EV share-of-new-sales figure could not be sourced; the 13% figure is a 2023 vintage.
entries.staleness: Policy targets CURRENT; the 13% EV sales-share datapoint is STALE (2023) — flagged gap

entries.topic: ADNOC Distribution — Shell Downstream South Africa acquisition
entries.finding: On 07-Jul-2026 ADNOC Distribution signed an agreement to acquire 100% of Shell Downstream South Africa for approximately USD 1bn enterprise value, covering ~580 Shell stations. The deal expands the network by roughly 55% to ~1,600 stations and increases fuel volumes by approximately 20%, to 19.2bn litres annually. Management expects it to be 6% EPS accretive from year one, to lift EBITDA by 13%, and to generate USD 30-40m of run-rate EBITDA synergies within five years. Completion is anticipated in 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. CEO Bader Al Lamki framed acquisition discipline as 'Is it value accretive or not? Can we add value to the business or not?', with Africa the primary focus and Southeast Asia also under consideration.
entries.source_name: ADNOC Distribution H1-2026 earnings call; Semafor — 'ADNOC wants more gas stations, eyes Africa and Southeast Asia'
entries.consequence: MATERIAL and UNRESOLVED at the valuation date. A USD 1bn EV acquisition against a AED 55.7bn (USD ~15.2bn) EV, adding ~55% to the network and ~20% to volumes, closing in 2027 — i.e. INSIDE the 5-year explicit forecast window but AFTER the last reported balance sheet. This is the study's clearest candidate for the mandatory dual-framing treatment: value the company BOTH ex-South Africa (standalone, no deal) AND pro-forma including it, published side by side, never averaged. It also introduces ZAR exposure and materially changes the debt build (funding is not disclosed; net debt/EBITDA is currently only 0.7x, so there is headroom). Confirm the funding structure and any disclosed purchase-price allocation from the company's own announcement before modelling.

entries.topic: ADNOC Distribution dividend policy
entries.finding: The dividend policy provides for an annual dividend of USD 700 million (20.57 fils per share) for the years 2024-2030, or a minimum of 75% of net profit, whichever is higher. The policy was extended through 2030. Track record since the 2017 IPO: USD 400m for 2018, USD 650m for 2019, and USD 700m for each of 2020-2024. Total dividends distributed since IPO: USD 5.8bn. From 2026 the company intends to pay dividends QUARTERLY for each fiscal year, a change from the prior semi-annual pattern. ADNOC's listed companies collectively target a record AED 158bn (USD 43bn) of dividends from 2025 to 2030.
entries.unit: USD million annual dividend floor (or 75% of net profit if higher), 2024-2030
entries.source_name: ADNOC Distribution — Dividends / Investor Relations; shareholder approval of the final 2025 dividend (April 2026)
entries.consequence: A contractual-strength, parent-endorsed policy running to 2030 — this is unusually firm for a dividend assumption and effectively fixes the payout leg of the model through the explicit forecast window. It also caps retained-earnings-funded growth: with a floor of the greater of USD 700m or 75% of net profit, the company distributes most of its earnings, so the South Africa acquisition (CO-05) and the station build must be debt-funded or funded from the 0.7x leverage headroom. The 'greater of' structure means the dividend RISES with profit but does not fall below USD 700m — a downside cushion worth pricing. The 5.05% trailing yield (CO-01) is a meaningful part of the total-return case.

entries.topic: ADNOC supply agreement — the 45 fils/litre minimum margin backstop
entries.finding: ADNOC Distribution's supply agreement with parent ADNOC for refined petroleum products includes a flexible pricing mechanism acting as a backstop guarantee. The agreement sets a fixed MINIMUM margin of approximately 45 fils per litre, guaranteeing a minimum profit level, with NO UPPER LIMIT — the company can earn more as retail prices rise. ADNOC compensates any margin shortfall versus the regulated margin. Separately, management explained on the H1-2026 call that the backstop protects against inventory losses on regulated UAE retail fuel sales when prices decline: it operates QUARTERLY and is CASH SETTLED, so if the company has a net loss on retail stocks in a quarter it charges the ADNOC Group. Management stated 'when prices come down, the backstop mechanism will essentially kick in' for the majority of retail inventory, and said the company chooses not to operate in declining-price environments within its COMMERCIAL segment to safeguard margins.
entries.unit: fils per litre minimum guaranteed margin (AED 0.45/litre)
entries.source_name: ADNOC Distribution H1-2026 earnings call, 05-Aug-2026; ADX filing on the ADNOC supply agreement
entries.consequence: THE most important structural feature of this business and the core of the valuation case. It converts a commodity-exposed retailer into something closer to a regulated utility with an option on price: a floor of ~45 fils/litre with unlimited upside. Three modelling consequences: (1) the downside case is bounded — even if crude collapses to the EIA's USD 65, UAE retail unit margin cannot fall below the floor, so the bear case should be built off 45 fils x volume, not off a proportional margin squeeze; (2) the H1-2026 inventory gain (CO-03) is the mirror image and will REVERSE via quarterly cash settlement as prices fall; (3) it justifies a materially LOWER equity beta and cost of capital than commodity peers, and is the strongest single argument for a premium to the EM fuel-distribution multiples (Vibra 7.7x, Ultrapar 6.8x). It is ALSO a related-party arrangement with a 77% parent — its renewal terms and duration are a key risk and must be read from the filings. The 45 fils figure is from secondary reporting of the ADX filing and MUST be confirmed against the supply agreement disclosure in the annual report before use.
entries.staleness: CURRENT as management commentary; the 45 fils figure requires primary confirmation

entries.topic: ADNOC Distribution debt and cost of debt evidence (CROSS-CHECK)
entries.finding: Company-level: ADNOC Distribution's board approved loan agreements worth approximately USD 2.25bn to refinance existing debt and for general corporate purposes; the company took a USD 375m term loan and a term facility of just over AED 4.13bn (USD 1.12bn) from FAB and other banks. No ADNOC Distribution-specific bond or sukuk issuance was located.
entries.unit: % profit rate, ADNOC Murban 10-year USD sukuk (PARENT, +60bp over UST)
entries.source_name: ADNOC — 'ADNOC Successfully Completes $1.5 Billion Debut International Sukuk Issuance'; AGBI on ADNOC Distribution loan facilities
entries.consequence: CROSS-CHECK for the marginal cost of debt. The Kd rule requires a MARGINAL, forward-looking rate in the CASH-FLOW CURRENCY (AED), sitting ABOVE the local sovereign. The parent's +60bp-over-UST sukuk spread is the best available corporate credit-spread evidence in the group; applied to the UAE federal AED curve (4.48% at ~4.5y, C-06) it implies an AED Kd of roughly 5.0-5.2% for the subsidiary — comfortably above the 4.48% sovereign, satisfying the rule. CAUTIONS: (i) the parent's spread is not the subsidiary's — ADNOC Distribution is 77%-owned but separately rated/unrated, so a modest additional spread is warranted; (ii) the sukuk is USD, the model is AED — the peg makes this close to equivalent but the basis should be stated; (iii) the USD 2.25bn loan facilities are bank debt at a floating EIBOR spread, not a fixed coupon, and the loan approval reporting is from 2022 and is STALE. GAP: ADNOC Distribution's own current debt stack, LC/FX split and average rate must be read from the filings per SIGCM clause 3 — this sweep does not resolve it.
entries.staleness: Parent sukuk MODERATELY STALE (May-2025); the USD 2.25bn loan facility reporting is STALE (2022). Company debt stack unresolved — flagged gap.

entries.topic: FTSE ADX General Index — the published index of the subject's own exchange
entries.finding: Daily index history for the FTSE ADX General Index, the headline capitalisation-weighted index of the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, covering 02-Jan-2011 to 24-Jul-2026 (3,884 sessions). Screened on its own terms rather than through the single-stock cleaning gate, which tests moves against an exchange daily price limit and has nothing to say about an index: no duplicate or out-of-order dates, no non-positive levels, largest single-session move 8.4% (March 2020), and a trading-day pattern that matches the exchange calendar on both sides of the January 2022 switch from a Sunday-to-Thursday week to Monday-to-Friday. Used as the market return in the beta regression: 257 weekly observations over the five years to 24-Jul-2026 give a beta of 0.649, R-squared 0.179, standard error 0.087.
entries.source_name: FTSE ADX General Index daily history
entries.consequence: Sets the beta, and through it the cost of equity, the cost of capital and the terminal cost of capital. Replaces the equal-weight composite of exchange members the first edition used as a stand-in for the index. The two are not interchangeable: the composite's weekly volatility is 1.34 times the published index's, and because beta divides covariance by the market's own variance, the more volatile stand-in produced a systematically LOWER beta — 0.507 against 0.649 — on an almost unchanged correlation (0.44 against 0.42). The stand-in was biased low by construction, not by chance.
entries.staleness: index level series; the beta is re-measured whenever the window rolls
